revisions.title: Divine credit, human inquiry
revisions.body: The opening puts lawgiving under divine credit: Kleinias names Zeus for Crete and Apollo for Sparta, and calls that the most just answer (obs_laws_0001). I hear the rest of this opening as a deliberate counter-movement: the claim is not left standing as a final explanation. The road becomes a way of imagining inquiry itself—conversation can proceed by pauses, questions, and shared effort, even when the travelers begin from inherited reverence.

revisions.title: From war to the question of rule
revisions.body: Cleinias’s war-centered account is still a thesis under examination, not the Athenian’s settled conclusion. The Athenian stretches its logic from city against city down to village, household, individual, and self; then reverses the direction, asking how a city divided between better and worse should be judged. The alternatives concern rule: destroy the bad, or let the good govern while the bad submit willingly. A third judge is then announced as a possibility.

revisions.title: The standard of lawgiving: reconciliation, not victory
revisions.body: The opening analogy supplies the standard: the best judge destroys none of the divided kin, but reconciles them and makes friendship durable through law. The Athenian carries that standard into politics, ranking reconciliation and civil peace above factional victory. Tyrtaeus is introduced as a witness to be questioned; his martial praise is set against a broader account of excellence in the harder war, changing what a lawgiver must seek.

revisions.title: Courage on both fronts
revisions.body: The unit begins as a numbered model for examining virtue, with Spartan practices offered as examples of endurance. It then widens courage’s field: the Athenian asks whether courage must resist pleasures as well as pains, and Megillus agrees. Read carefully, the closing challenge tests whether the speakers can point to comparable laws; it should not be inflated into proof that Crete or Sparta has none.

revisions.title: A Protected Space for Critiquing the Cities' Laws
revisions.body: The Athenian is not opening a general license for old men to criticize whenever the young are away. He describes a protocol: criticism of the interlocutors’ cities’ laws belongs before a magistrate or an age-mate, never before the young; here, the speakers’ age and the absence of youth make the exchange permissible. The inquiry then tests Megillus’s tentative praise of common meals and gymnasia against the Athenian’s mixed assessment of their benefits and dangers.

revisions.title: The test is the governed drinking party
revisions.body: The Athenian changes the test for judging a practice. Victory and defeat are too disputed to settle its worth; we must ask how the practice is conducted and under what kind of ruler. Applied to the drinking party, the method blocks a verdict based only on badly managed examples. The section ends by opening a broader question: what benefit, if any, follows when drinking is rightly governed?

revisions.title: Education, then the golden law
revisions.body: The section separates two stages that should not be collapsed. First, the Athenian defines education as childhood nurture that turns play, pleasure, and desire toward the virtue of a future adult and citizen; this is a definition of education’s aim, not yet an account of the soul’s competing impulses. The puppet image then changes the question: pleasure and pain pull against one another, while calculation is named the city’s common law. The golden leading-string is therefore not law assisting calculation; it is calculation figured as the law’s gentle, guiding cord. Education forms the desires, while law gives the rational guide public authority.

revisions.title: The lawgiver’s wine test
revisions.body: Wine is a paradoxical instrument: it weakens judgment, yet that exposure may become a trial of character. The Athenian makes drunkenness childlike and least self-controlled, then asks us to seek a later benefit as with bodily hardship. Read the final move as a lawgiver’s thought experiment, not a celebration: the citizen must be both fearless and fearful, with shame opposing pleasures that undo self-command.

revisions.title: Egypt, imitation, and educated pleasure
revisions.body: Egypt is offered as a precedent for fixing musical forms and resisting innovation. But one way to hear the Athenian’s move is not as the demolition of pleasure: he rejects the crude equation of musical correctness with whatever pleases a soul, because choral performances imitate character, and enjoyment can assimilate a person to what is enjoyed. Pleasure remains a criterion, now answerable to the best and adequately educated hearer.

revisions.title: From judging pleasure to teaching justice
revisions.body: The crucial movement is from judging pleasure to forming it. The true judge teaches rather than follows the crowd, while songs are treated as soul-charms that train the young to share the law’s pleasures and pains. When the Athenian turns to the just life, he frames happiness for the temperate and just, and misery for the wealthy unjust, as what poets are to teach. Read this as a demand for civic affirmation, not as knowingly false instruction.

revisions.title: From persuasive myth to age-graded song
revisions.body: The unit's hinge is the movement from persuasion to institution. The Sidonian story supplies the example: even an improbable tale can help a lawgiver shape young souls. The proposed response is age-graded singing, not a three-part Dionysian chorus for the whole population: those no longer able to carry a song are left to tell stories, while wine is proposed for men over forty as an aid to older participation.

revisions.title: Music judged by imitation, not pleasure
revisions.body: The argument gives music a stricter test than immediate enjoyment. Since musical works are imitations, the judge must know the original, assess the copy’s correctness, and recognize how well it is made; pleasure cannot do that work. The older singers therefore need more thorough training than the majority or the poets, including the fuller judgment required to guide younger listeners toward virtue.

revisions.title: Wine as a governed exercise
revisions.body: The hinge here is conditional, not celebratory: the Athenian allows wine a civic place only when a symposium is treated as a serious, law-governed exercise in temperance. Sober Dionysian overseers guide the un-sober, and the promised result is that participants leave better friends rather than enemies. Hear the test being set: wine is useful only when an institution gives pleasure a form.

revisions.title: From patriarchal custom to legislation
revisions.body: Book 3 asks us to watch political order emerge, not appear whole. After catastrophe, the survivors are cut off from city arts and writing, but they are not without rule: they live by custom and patriarchal law. Separate clans preserve inherited usages; when settlements enlarge, representatives compare those usages and turn selected customs into legislation. The point is developmental: constitutional order grows by consolidating older forms, with Homer serving as witness.

revisions.title: When desire disagrees with judgment
revisions.body: Here the Athenian makes prayer answer to a problem inside the soul. The greatest ignorance is not merely lacking a skill; it is a divided will: reasoned judgment calls something noble and good while pleasure and pain turn toward its opposite. That is why the common wish for everything to obey us is unsafe as a prayer. The desired end must be governed by phronesis and nous, or it may become the opposite of what we wanted.

revisions.title: The cure is cumulative
revisions.body: At 690d the catalogue of rival titles to rule becomes a diagnosis of faction. But the Lacedaemonian case is not presented as kingship saved by one divine dilution. The Athenian’s retrospective sequence is cumulative: a god makes the royal line twin; a human element joined to divine power adds the council of elders; then a third saviour adds the ephors. The resulting mixture is measured enough for kingship to survive and to become a cause of safety for others. Read the theology here as the passage’s way of narrating institutional balance, not as a single-cause explanation.

revisions.title: Persia’s reversal across generations
revisions.body: Persia’s story is a reversal, not a single slide into decay. Under Cyrus, measured freedom and shared counsel make the regime prosper; then the Athenian asks how it was lost under Cambyses and nearly saved under Darius. Darius stands apart: not a king’s son, not luxuriously reared, he uses law to secure fellowship. The warning is about succession and education across generations—not about making every later ruler a son of Cyrus.

revisions.title: From regime labels to a proposed rule of law
revisions.body: Cleinias and Megillus cannot settle Sparta or Knossos under the familiar labels. The Athenian’s correction is that these names identify cities by the part that dominates them. The Cronus account is presented as a reported model, not a finished constitution; its practical proposal is to order public and private life by reason, and call that ordering law.

revisions.title: Honor is measured by betterment
revisions.body: The speech makes “honor” answerable to what it does. The soul stands immediately after the gods, yet self-praise, blame-shifting, indulgence in pleasure, yielding to fear, preference for beauty over virtue, and dishonorable pursuit of wealth all damage what they claim to honor. The test is not the appearance of esteem but whether one’s conduct makes the soul better.

revisions.title: Preparing the hearer for law
revisions.body: The teaching point here is preparation, not inventory. Before the laws are stated, praise and blame are supposed to make people tractable and well-disposed toward them (obs_laws_0567). I would therefore hear the later comparison of lives as persuasion toward a law-shaped ideal, not as a pleasure-only proof or a special argument for unbelievers; that reading also fits the unit’s preference for noble lifelong service to home laws over contest victory (claim_laws_0355).

revisions.title: Purity as a founding premise
revisions.body: One way to hear this turn is as a verbal bracket around purification. The herd analogy makes cleansing a lawgiver’s concern, but the present founding is not assigned a colony or a selection by purification. I take the next premise—that the collection is complete and its purity secured—as a stipulation, not a report of an already-purified citizen body. The question becomes: what institutional design can begin once purity is assumed?

revisions.title: The second-best polity as an approximation
revisions.body: The city where friends’ things are common is the paradigm, not the immediate settlement; the polity being attempted is second-best. Its approximation of unity is institutional: allotted land is regarded as common to the city, households remain fixed, and the original measure of property is protected from buying and selling. The closing lesson is ethical: extreme wealth cannot make anyone good or happy.

revisions.title: Designing the ideal, then adjusting it
revisions.body: Here the Athenian treats founding as a problem of design rather than a single stroke of inspiration. Unequal starting wealth is organized through proportionate property assessments, while the land is divided into twelve parts and each lot joins near and distant ground to compensate for unequal terrain. The resulting city is a pattern, not a guarantee: when an ideal detail proves impossible, legislation should pursue the closest fitting alternative.

revisions.title: The first offices are a provisional bridge
revisions.body: Here the Athenian makes officeholding the test of legislation: well-framed laws can be made useless and harmful by unsuitable magistrates. The colony cannot simply solve that problem through its first election, because its settlers are strangers to one another and uneducated in the laws. Knossos is therefore assigned founding help, beginning with thirty-seven law-guardians drawn from Knossians and settlers. This is a provisional bridge, not a solved bootstrap: after time and constitutional endurance, a more public, staged election is proposed.

revisions.title: Sacred appointment and territorial guardianship
revisions.body: Here the law separates sacred appointment from sacred interpretation: priests are assigned by lot after scrutiny, but the exegetes are nominated and voted for by the tribes, then sent to Delphi for the god to select one from each triad. The unit then extends its guarding scheme from civic offices to a rotating rural service.

revisions.title: Civic formation and differentiated judgment
revisions.body: Education is presented as the greatest of the city’s highest offices, because early formation is treated as decisive. The courts then distribute judgment by kind of case, not through one three-tier ladder: private disputes have a third-stage common court whose judges are selected by the offices, while private suits use tribal courts with jurors chosen by lot. Public indictments give the people the beginning and end of trial, with examination by three high offices.

revisions.title: The lawgiver’s unfinished work
revisions.body: Read this passage as a test of whether legislation can survive its maker. The painter analogy proposes that a work meant to improve needs a successor who can repair damage and finish what its maker missed. The Athenian turns that condition into a civic task: because the founders are old and the guardians young, the guardians must become future legislators and law-guardians, filling out the laws’ outline.

revisions.title: The limit of written marriage law
revisions.body: The important turn here is not a list of wedding regulations but a limit on what written law can accomplish. A man becomes eligible at twenty-five and must marry before thirty-five, yet he is first given a prelude on how to seek what is fitting. The city wants marriages to temper wealth and character, but the result in children cannot be directly seen; persuasion and reproach therefore do work that blunt compulsion cannot.

revisions.title: When law must become lived practice
revisions.body: One way to hear this whole turn is as a test of whether law can become lived practice. It begins with a dispute that is both practical and verbal—what is said about slaves cuts against need and follows it—and sharpens into a demand that conduct toward the powerless reveal genuine justice. The later shift to the new city distinguishes the order of speaking from the order of building. The question is not whether a rule sounds orderly, but whether people can inhabit it.

revisions.title: A Reforming Ideal Meets Civic Habit
revisions.body: Here the Athenian turns women’s common meals into a test of legislation: he calls their omission an error and proposes practices shared by women and men for the city’s happiness. But the proposal is not presented as universally ready to impose. Where a city has not recognized common meals at all, even mentioning public eating for women would meet resistance. The passage holds reforming principle against institutional circumstance.

revisions.title: Play as the first civic discipline
revisions.body: The Athenian treats children’s play as the first place where civic order can be learned, not as a harmless interval before education. From ages three to six, children gather for shared games at village shrines, while nurses and appointed women supervise their conduct. I read this arrangement as a political decision: the city begins shaping common habits precisely where children experience themselves as merely playing.

revisions.title: A standard for selective reading
revisions.body: The issue here is not a ban on poetry but a test for what young people should absorb. The Athenian warns that memorizing whole poets or anthologies is dangerous because poets speak both well and badly. He therefore makes the Laws’ own measured speeches a model, while allowing other verse or prose only when it is genuinely akin to them. Read the move as a demand for selection, not as a rejection of poetry.

revisions.title: Praise, blame, and bounded permission
revisions.body: Here hunting tests the lawgiver’s two registers: praise and blame shape the young, while the final rule marks actual permissions. The preferred hunt is not merely horse and hound but quadruped pursuit using horses, dogs, and the hunter’s own body. Yet fowling and water-hunting are not simply banned: each remains allowed in specified places and under stated restrictions.

revisions.title: Peace as the training ground
revisions.body: Here the Athenian turns peace from the opposite of war into its training ground. A good city’s peaceful life is not secured by neglecting conflict, but by rehearsing it while peace still holds: monthly campaigns, festive battles, and the athlete’s daily practice prepare citizens for the real contest over their lives, children, property, and city.

revisions.title: The virtue test for erotic law
revisions.body: The section tests erotic law by its contribution to virtue. A nature-based argument is acknowledged as potentially persuasive but misaligned with the interlocutors’ cities; the Athenian then asks what the practice contributes to virtue. After distinguishing body-, soul-, and mixed-oriented loves, he frames the legal choice as selective. An adjacent example makes enforcement concrete: an unwritten norm gains force when the whole city repeats its shameful, god-hated character.

revisions.title: Land-based sustenance, then agricultural law
revisions.body: Here the Stranger links institutional design to the city’s material base: most Greek cities draw sustenance from land and sea, whereas this city is described as land-based. He therefore says the legislator can leave many maritime and commercial matters aside and turn to agriculture. That is narrower than a general ban on trade: the passage presents a legislative focus, then begins agricultural law with boundary protection before divine and civic judgment.

revisions.title: When education must admit a limit
revisions.body: Here the lawgiver confronts a limit in the city’s educational hope. A well-raised citizen is not expected to commit sacrilege, yet human beings may prove resistant even to strong laws, so the city must legislate for that failure. The prelude before the penalty is the key: law first addresses disordered desire and directs it toward rites and good company. Read the ensuing punishments as the boundary of education, not its simple replacement.

revisions.title: Retaining the legal distinction, refining its meaning
revisions.body: The Athenian does not discard the law’s voluntary/involuntary categories. He insists that they must be defined before penalties can be judged, then separates harm from injustice: an unwilled injury is not automatically an injustice, and law must repair damage while trying to restore civic friendship. The shift is therefore not replacement, but clarification.

revisions.title: Agency, not a binary
revisions.body: Listen for the code’s governing question: not simply whether a death occurred, but what kind of agency produced it. The law limits penalties for acts committed in a diminished condition while retaining a distinct homicide consequence, and it places anger-killings between voluntary and involuntary homicide. One way to read the stretch is as a search for proportion, not a single rule for every killing.

revisions.title: When law must persuade
revisions.body: At 885b, the legal catalogue turns into a diagnosis: impiety is presented through three positions—denying gods, denying their care for humans, or treating them as persuadable by sacrifice and prayer. The imagined offenders demand persuasion before threats, while Clinias says a persuasive theological prelude matters more than brevity. One way to hear the shift is as a test of law’s reach: before punishing conduct, it must address the beliefs behind it.

revisions.title: From cosmology to civic persuasion
revisions.body: Read this section as a movement from explanation to legislation. The reported account explains the elements and living things without mind, god, or art, treats gods and justice as products of convention, and connects that teaching with force, impiety, and faction. The Athenian then poses, rather than settles, whether law should pair penalties with persuasion.

revisions.title: From motion to soul
revisions.body: One way to hear this unit is as a shift from classification to priority. The exchange first sorts motion by place and encounter, then adds two kinds expressly for the inquiry into soul. Self-moving motion is promoted to first and strongest because a chain of motions moved by others cannot supply its beginning. Soul is then identified with that motion and placed before body.

revisions.title: The third proposition: divine justice is not for sale
revisions.body: Here the argument tests its third proposition: that gods cannot be turned aside from justice by gifts. The Athenian makes the contrary picture absurd by comparing bribable gods to wolves taming dogs with stolen plunder, and to pilots or charioteers who betray their task. He then asks whether the three propositions have been adequately demonstrated; Kleinias agrees. The passage presents this as their conclusion; the record does not independently verify the earlier proofs.

revisions.title: When law withdraws its protection
revisions.body: This unit repeatedly makes legal protection depend on public procedure rather than private trust. A disputed object is kept with magistrates until judgment; an exchange made outside the appointed market or without immediate payment is left to the parties’ confidence, not ordinary legal action. One way to read the pattern is that the law protects commerce by making its conditions visible before the bargain is made.

revisions.title: Making family protection public
revisions.body: The governing thread here is the publicization of family protection. Orphanhood is framed as a second birth: law-guardians stand in for begetters, while guardians must care for the ward no less than for their own children; neglect is exposed to penalties and suits. The same principle governs disowning: a father cannot sever a son by private anger alone, but must face a kin-group hearing, equal replies, and a majority vote. One way to read the sequence is that household authority remains real, but never wholly private.

revisions.title: From hidden harm to public speech
revisions.body: One way to hear the governing movement of this stretch is as a widening account of harm: from bodily poisoning and ritual practices that persuade both would-be agents and frightened victims, to penalties calibrated by expertise and future correction. The rule against reviling turns dispute toward teaching; the later bans on public ridicule and comic treatment extend that concern into civic speech and performance.

revisions.title: Judging the kind of fault
revisions.body: The section’s governing question is not the size of the violation or the bare fact of loss, but the kind of fault the case reveals. Public theft is judged through the offender’s supposed curability, while arms-loss is divided between voluntary abandonment and forcible deprivation. That distinction is the unit’s legal and moral hinge.

revisions.title: Making a ruler of rulers
revisions.body: Here the Athenian makes the auditor a “ruler of rulers”: the office must exceed the officials it judges in virtue, not merely outrank them. Then comes the revealing compromise. This supposedly superior authority is assembled through public nomination, voting, age rules, and lot. I hear the passage testing whether a city can institutionalize moral superiority without pretending that civic selection has made its candidates divine.

revisions.title: The city’s gate has rules
revisions.body: Read this passage as a case for controlled contact, not isolation. The danger is the ungoverned introduction of innovations into a well-ordered city; total refusal would also make it appear harsh. Ordinary private travel is barred below forty, while public missions remain possible. More deliberate inspection belongs to reputable citizens over fifty and under sixty, who return to confirm sound laws and correct omissions—not to copy foreign practices wholesale.

revisions.title: Keeping legal power public
revisions.body: This long run can be heard as a test of whether private advantage may bend public process. The searcher must swear and search naked or ungirt; forceful obstruction can void a proceeding and trigger penalties; and service to the fatherland must be performed without gifts. One way to read the sequence is that law protects trust by making access, procedure, and public service answerable to the common rule.

revisions.title: Funeral law as a discipline of the living
revisions.body: Across this unit, funeral law keeps death from taking more than the living can spare: graves are kept off workable soil, monuments and spending are capped, and public mourning is confined. The passage then states its rationale: the dead cannot receive great help, so relatives should have helped while the person was alive. I hear the whole passage as a law of proportion—grief is permitted, but it must not impoverish the living.
